# C202 Chapter 1 Study Guide: Strategic Human Resource Management

*A 15-20 minute read, organized by the chapter's sections in order. Read it before drilling the deck. Each concept covers what it is, why it matters, an example, and how it connects to the rest of the chapter.*

## How this chapter maps to your competencies

This chapter falls under **Strategic Human Resource Management**: *determining the strategic impact of HRM on the organization*. Chapters 1 and 2 together make up about 14% of the Objective Assessment (OA). Expect questions that ask you to judge how an HR choice helps or hurts a company's strategy, not just to define terms. A few ideas preview other competencies: compensation types (1.9) return under **Motivational Concepts**, performance management (1.8) under **Effective HRM**, and employment law (1.4) under **Legal and Regulatory Requirements** in Chapter 3.

Chapter 1 is part of **Quarter 1** (Chapters 1-4), which ends with a quarterly quiz. WGU's strongest readiness signal for the Pre-Assessment is scoring **80% or higher** on the final e-text quiz.

## 1.1-1.3 Why this chapter matters: people are the advantage

### Competitive advantage

**Competitive advantage** means doing something differently from your competitors in a way that lets you outperform them. Companies chase it through technology, products, location, low cost, or great service.

*Why it matters:* The chapter's central claim is that people create and sustain every one of those sources. A clever product gets copied. A low-cost process stalls if workers don't run it well. Great service is nothing more than employees treating customers well. So whoever attracts, develops, and keeps the best talent tends to win, especially in knowledge-based businesses where the employees' expertise *is* the product.

*Example:* Two coffee shops buy the same machines and beans. The one with better-trained, more engaged baristas wins the loyal customers.

*Connection:* Everything else in the chapter explains *how* HR turns people into that advantage.

### The opening case: Patagonia

Patagonia makes outdoor clothing, and its mission centers on building the best product, causing no unnecessary harm, and using business to address environmental problems. It is a certified B Corp and a major environmental donor.

*Why it matters:* HR's job is to build a culture that reinforces Patagonia's strategy. The chapter returns to this case in 1.20.

## 1.4 What is HRM?

### Definition

**Human resource management (HRM)** is the function responsible for attracting, hiring, developing, rewarding, and retaining talent. It also handles people issues and makes sure the company complies with employment laws.

*Why it matters:* Employee costs are one of the biggest items in most budgets, so how a firm manages people has a huge financial impact. HRM's ultimate purpose is to **manage risk** (legal, financial, cultural) and to **build a talent system that keeps great employees**.

*A quick history:* The first "personnel" department appeared at National Cash Register in 1901, after a strike, and focused on payroll, safety, and compliance. HR later added labor relations, recruiting, training, and, since the 1980s, change and culture. Today technology and outsourcing absorb much of the paperwork, which frees HR to act strategically.

### The should do / can do / will do model

This is the chapter's most important framework. HRM shapes performance by influencing three things:

1. **What employees should do.** This is *direction*. Business strategy, competition, and laws shape it. **HR planning** designs work so it's efficient and forecasts how many and what kinds of people the company will need. Employment laws (many of which exist because of past discrimination) set limits on what employers can do.
2. **What employees can do.** This is *ability*. Recruiting and staffing bring in people with the right ability and motivation, and training builds their skills. Example: when a hospital buys a new machine, nurses need training before they *can* use it.
3. **What employees will do.** This is *motivation*. Compensation and performance management push effort in a direction.

*Why it matters:* All three must be in place and pointing the same way. When they are, you get effective work processes (strategy gets executed, the environment is positive, employees are engaged). That produces competitive advantage, which produces organizational performance.

*The foundation is "can do":* Staffing and development come first because incentives can't create ability. You can't bonus someone into skills they don't have.

*Warning about "will do":* Rewards can drive the wrong behavior. Subprime mortgage brokers earned bonuses for risky loans. In 2016 Wells Fargo fired more than 5,000 employees who opened fake customer accounts to hit sales quotas. The lesson: when you design rewards, ask what behavior they might *accidentally* encourage.

*How HRM creates value:* It cuts people-related costs (turnover, lawsuits), improves service and client relationships, and improves product cost and quality.

*Everyday example:* A new server needs to know the service standards (should), be trained on the ordering system (can), and have a reason to upsell, like tips (will).

## 1.5 What does HRM do? The six functions

HRM designs systems that acquire, motivate, develop, and retain talent. The chapter groups that work into six functions:

1. Staffing
2. Training and development
3. Performance management
4. Rewards and benefits
5. Health and safety
6. Employee-management relations

*Connection:* Each one maps onto the should/can/will model. Staffing and training mostly drive "can do," and rewards and performance management drive "will do." The next six sections cover each function, and the chapter keeps stressing that they depend on one another.

## 1.6 Staffing

**Staffing** is planning, acquiring, deploying, and retaining employees so the organization has the talent it needs to carry out its **business strategy**. It moves talent *into*, *through*, and *out of* the company.

*The steps:* identify job requirements, then source candidates, recruit them (attract them, keep them interested, get them to accept), retain and move people within the company, and finally manage **separations**: terminations for performance, layoffs, restructuring, and resignations. Separations are part of staffing, a point the quiz tests.

*Why it matters:* A wrong hire is hard to fix. Training and pay can't make up for someone who lacks the basic ability or fit for the job.

*Example:* At Caribou Coffee, district managers who carefully staffed their store manager roles saw stronger revenue.

*Connection:* Staffing supplies the raw talent that training and performance management work with, so it directly affects both. (Chapters 5 and 6 go deeper on recruiting and selection.)

## 1.7 Training and development

**Training and development** builds employees' capabilities through formal and informal learning. It also covers career planning, organizational development, and compliance training (for example, teaching managers how to interview and terminate legally).

*Why it matters:* Training is how a company keeps skills current. It can be wasted, though: if a hire can't succeed, or quits before the company recoups the cost, the money is gone. Some retail jobs see turnover around 200% a year.

*Connection:* Training only pays off when it's aligned with performance management and rewards. If reviews and pay don't recognize new skills, people won't use them. HRM is a system of functions that reinforce each other.

### Succession planning

**Succession planning** prepares people in advance to step into key positions, which reduces disruption when someone leaves.

*Example:* Citigroup started searching for a CEO only after its leader left, and the company drifted. Google worked with Sundar Pichai for years; he became Google's CEO in 2015 and Alphabet's CEO in 2019, which made the handoff smooth. CEO succession is the role companies most often overlook.

## 1.8 Performance management

**Performance management** aligns employees' goals and behaviors with the organization's goals and strategy. It also appraises past and current performance and suggests ways to improve.

*Why it matters:* It's how strategy shows up in each person's job. It's often tied to pay, so biased or inaccurate ratings demotivate people quickly.

*What makes it work:* **Specific goals** and **frequent feedback**. Goals tell people what to aim for; feedback tells them how they're doing so they can adjust.

- Without goals, focus is unclear, people underperform, and some quit, which creates more work for staffing.
- Without accurate feedback, people can't adjust. Feedback that feels unfair lowers effort.
- **Performance feedback** also maintains ethical behavior and communicates expectations. This is the answer to the quiz question about which kind of feedback supports ethics.

*Connection:* Performance management depends on staffing for talent and on development to close gaps, and it feeds the rewards system.

## 1.9 Rewards and benefits

Pay that feels adequate and fair drives motivation, performance, and retention.

### Total rewards

**Total rewards** is the sum of everything an employee receives for their time, effort, and performance. It has three parts:

1. **Direct financial compensation:** salary, wages, commissions, bonuses, and stock options.
2. **Indirect financial compensation (benefits):** health insurance, wellness programs, paid vacation, free meals, and retirement plans.
3. **Nonfinancial compensation:** intrinsic rewards from the job or workplace, like feeling successful, appreciated, or proud of your work. The textbook shows this as roughly half of total rewards.

*Why it matters:* Compare job offers on total rewards, not salary alone. A lower salary with strong retirement matching, health coverage, and training can be worth more.

*Connection to staffing:* Pay level and hiring influence each other. Premium pay lets a company recruit top candidates. Low pay may force it to hire less-prepared people and then raise pay or train more. Incentive pay also depends on accurate performance management and on staffing and training supplying ability.

*Example:* Costco pays roughly twice the market rate, more than rival Sam's Club. Because turnover is lower and productivity higher, its labor returns are similar, and customers get a better experience. Top pay isn't always necessary (does every marketer need an MBA?), but it can be an advantage.

## 1.10 Health and safety

This function covers wellness, accident and injury prevention, ergonomics, disaster preparedness, bullying, and violence. **Workplace safety** protects employees from toxins, accidents, and injuries. **Workplace health** covers physical *and* mental health; job instability and heavy workloads raise stress.

*Why it matters:* A healthy, safe workplace is the ethical thing to do, and it also pays. It raises productivity, lowers health care and workers' compensation premiums, and cuts lost time. Many federal and state laws apply.

*Example:* A warehouse that provides safety gear, trains workers to use it, and holds people accountable avoids injuries, downtime, and insurance spikes.

## 1.11 Employee-management relations

**Employee-management relations** reflects society's beliefs about the relationship between workers and owners, and it defines the employment rights of both sides.

*Why it matters:* Positive relations improve communication, problem solving, and performance, in union and non-union workplaces alike. Tools include participation programs and employee surveys. In unionized settings, employers must bargain in good faith, and a collective bargaining agreement sets the terms. In 2019 about 33.6% of public-sector workers were union members, versus 6.2% in the private sector.

### Alignment of HR functions

The six functions must be **consistent in what they reinforce** and must not undermine each other.

*Example of misalignment:* A company trains teamwork but pays only for individual results. Employees follow the money.

*Example of alignment:* SAS, an analytics company, treats employees as its most valuable asset. Its trust-based culture, results-focused performance management, and generous benefits (on-site medical care, tuition reimbursement, flexible schedules) all point the same way. The result is low turnover and decades on "best places to work" lists.

## 1.12 How HRM influences organizational performance

### Two ways HRM adds value

HRM adds value by improving **efficiency** (efficient systems and processes) or by contributing to **revenue growth**. The chapter calls HR an underused source of advantage. Effective HR systems also:

- clarify responsibilities in light of the mission
- develop capabilities and use skills efficiently
- link rewards fairly to responsibility and performance
- raise engagement and effort
- improve change management
- reduce bad outcomes like turnover and legal liability

*Quiz trap:* "Reporting ethics breaches to the Bureau of Labor Statistics" is *not* one of these outcomes.

### Four types of HR risk

1. **Strategic risk:** talent strategy, culture, ethics, people investments, and change. *Example:* rapid growth erodes the ethical culture.
2. **Operational risk:** how quickly and well you hire, develop, and keep top performers. *Example:* key roles sit unfilled and projects stall.
3. **Financial risk:** pay, benefits, turnover, overtime, and costly errors or accidents. *Example:* overtime costs double.
4. **Compliance risk:** diversity, safety, unions, whistleblowers, and harassment. *Example:* managers were never trained on harassment policy.

### Small organizations

Firms with fewer than 500 workers employ about half the U.S. workforce, yet many have no HR budget or trained managers. Poor HR practices are a leading cause of small-business failure, so HR is an investment, not just a cost.

## 1.13 The role of HRM in executing business strategy

### Business strategy and fit

**Business strategy** is how a company competes. It reflects what customers want, what the company wants, and what it can deliver cost-effectively, and it can differ across business units. The key idea is **fit**: HR must fit the business strategy, and the strategy must fit the competitive environment. Competitive advantage comes from using resources and capabilities, mostly talent, to create superior value.

### Talent philosophy

A **talent philosophy** is a company's system of beliefs about how employees should be treated. It covers the value of diversity, ethics, short-term versus career-long employment, and whether employees are assets or "investors" of their time. Founders usually shape it: are employees partners to develop, or replaceable parts? *(On the quiz, "employee philosophy" is the tempting wrong answer.)*

*Example:* Goldman Sachs calls its people its greatest asset.

### HR strategy vs. strategic HRM

- **Human resource strategy** links the entire HR function to the business strategy.
- **Strategic HRM** aligns the company's values and goals with employees' behaviors, values, and goals, and it shapes the strategy of each HR function.

*Connection:* When the functions are aligned this way, they form an **integrated HRM system** guided by the talent philosophy. This is the "alignment" idea from 1.11, viewed from the strategy level.

## 1.14 Global issues

HR has to adapt to strategy, local labor markets, and different cultural values around the world.

### Global mindset

A **global mindset** is the set of personal attributes that lets you influence people and organizations from very different social, cultural, and institutional systems. You build it through experience. One expert calls basic business skills "table stakes" and cross-cultural influence the real differentiator. HSBC sends new managers on long international assignments to develop it.

### Culture and power distance

Cultures differ in what motivates people, how directly they communicate, and how they balance family and work. **Power distance**, the acceptance of hierarchy, is small in the U.S., Sweden, and Germany and large in Japan and Mexico. Managers in high power-distance cultures are less likely to empower employees or enrich jobs.

*Example:* A "challenge your boss" program that works in Sweden may flop in a high power-distance country. The lesson is to match HR practices to the local culture.

## 1.15 Gaining a competitive advantage through HRM

Michael Porter says advantage comes from offering superior customer value: either a better product at a premium price or a good product at a lower price. Different advantages need different HR approaches:

- **Operational excellence** (low cost): lean pay and benefits, teamwork, consistent procedures, and tight cost control. *Example:* a budget airline.
- **Product innovation** (Apple, 3M, Nintendo, pharma): an innovative culture and hires with teamwork, analytical, and creative skills who persist through failure.
- **Customer intimacy, or customization** (consulting, retail, banking): deep customer knowledge and flexible service. Starbucks charges a premium and invests heavily in hiring active learners with customer skills and emotional resilience.
- **Growth** (Chipotle, Panera): develop and acquire talent, either organically by opening locations or through **mergers and acquisitions (M&A)**. M&A is a common route to international expansion.

*Why M&A fails:* Most often the problem is **culture clash**, not technical or financial issues. DaimlerChrysler, HP-Compaq, and AOL-Time Warner are the classic examples. Check culture, values, and structure fit before the deal.

*Connection:* Whatever the strategy, retention and engagement sustain it (Southwest Airlines, SAS).

## 1.16 Who is responsible for HRM?

HR is shared across many players, and technology increasingly pushes HR tasks to managers and employees.

- **HR professionals:** strategic partners, not "police." They align the talent philosophy and HR strategy with the business, build managers' HR skills, need business acumen (how the company makes money), and lead **organizational change** such as expansion, restructuring, and downsizing.
- **Managers:** every supervising manager does HRM daily. HR supplies tools like interview guides and review forms, but those only add value if managers use them well. Mattel made managers partners in managing talent.
- **Employees:** they increasingly own their own development and keep their skills records current. **Employee handbooks** document HR policies, and good **communication** between HR and employees is essential.
- **Shared service centers:** in-house hubs that centralize routine transactions like payroll and benefits to cut cost and improve consistency (Home Depot's HR call centers).
- **Outside vendors:** outsourcing payroll, benefits, or relocation is often smart, especially for small firms, because vendors bring expertise and better pricing.
- **Professional employer organizations (PEOs):** they lease workers to client firms for about 2-7% of gross wages and become the *legal employer*, handling payroll, benefits, training, and discipline. The client gains flexibility; in a downturn it simply doesn't renew the lease.

## 1.17 Case study: HR transformation at IBM

IBM operates in more than 170 countries. Its HR goal was the right talent, at the right time, in the right place. IBM split HR into **core roles** (policy design, internal consulting) and **administrative roles** (payroll, expenses, records). It centralized admin work in global service centers and automated repeatable processes.

*Why it matters:* Freeing HR from paperwork let it focus on hiring, upskilling, leadership development, and compensation, which is exactly the shift from administrative to strategic HR described in 1.4. IBM also replaced the annual review with flexible goals and frequent feedback, including peer feedback, through Checkpoint, an app employees helped design. That connects to the goals-and-feedback lesson from 1.8.

## 1.18 Ethics in HRM

The **Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM)**, the largest HR professional association, publishes a code of ethical and professional standards. HR professionals should add value and support ethical success, take responsibility for their decisions, and advocate for the profession. The guidelines include holding high ethical standards, measuring HR's effectiveness, obeying the law, serving with social responsibility, advocating for proper treatment of people, and advocating openly through proper channels.

*Example:* If a leader pressures HR to bury a safety complaint, the code points toward escalating it properly.

## 1.19 Human resource management systems and careers

A **human resource management system (HRMS)** is a technology platform that securely stores employee records (payroll, benefits), tracks recruiting and staffing, and runs analytics. It can be cloud-based (Workday, Cornerstone OnDemand) or built in-house. Choose one based on how you'll actually use it and how easy it is for managers and employees. Modern systems integrate apps and support continuous feedback.

*Careers:* HR jobs were projected to grow faster than average, and hiring, motivating, and retaining people are great-manager skills in any field.

## 1.20 Patagonia's response

Patagonia calls itself "a cause disguised as a company," and its HR practices put that culture into action:

- **Hiring:** interviews start with "what drew you here?" to find community-minded people who add to the culture.
- **Benefits that reinforce the mission:** up to two months of paid environmental volunteering after a year, bail support for peaceful environmental protest, and subsidized on-site childcare. The childcare helps nearly all new mothers return to work.
- **Results:** about 4% turnover and thousands of applicants for a handful of openings.

*Connection:* This is strategic HRM in action. The talent philosophy, staffing, and rewards all reinforce the business strategy.

## 1.22 Pulling it together

- People, not assets, explain why some firms outperform others. HRM turns potential into performance by shaping what employees **should**, **can**, and **will** do.
- The six functions must be aligned into one integrated system guided by a talent philosophy. Functions that conflict undermine strategy.
- How a firm positions itself determines the advantage it needs, and that determines its HR strategy.

## What to be able to explain

These are WGU's official Chapter 1 Learning Checklist items. You should be able to explain each one in a business context:

- Explain how HRM strategy supports a company's business strategy.
- Describe the six primary HRM functions and what they do.
- Explain why HRM is critical to a company’s overall performance.
- Identify the impact of misaligned HR functions (e.g., when rewards conflict with training).

To get there, make sure you can also explain:

- Should/can/will do, which functions drive each, and why "can do" is the foundation
- How a reward system can backfire (Wells Fargo)
- Direct vs. indirect vs. nonfinancial compensation
- The two ways HRM adds value and the four HR risk types
- How talent philosophy, HR strategy, and strategic HRM differ
- Which HR approach fits each competitive strategy, and why M&A often fails
- Who shares HR responsibility, and PEO vs. shared service center

cards.front: What is a global mindset, and how do you get one?
cards.answer: The ability to influence people from very different cultures and systems; it's built through experience.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.14 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.14 Global Issues
points: i4cp: cross-cultural influence matters more than basic business skills ('table stakes')
HSBC sends new managers on long international assignments to build it

cards.front: How should power distance shape HR practices in another country?
cards.answer: In high power-distance cultures, empowering employees can clash with norms, so practices should fit local culture.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.14 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.14 Global Issues
points: Small power distance: U.S., Sweden, Germany; large: Japan, Mexico
Cultures also differ in motivation, communication style, family vs work emphasis

cards.front: How do operational excellence and product innovation strategies need different HRM?
cards.answer: Operational excellence stresses cost control and consistency; innovation needs creative hires and room to experiment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.15 Gaining a Competitive Advantage Through HRM
points: Operational excellence: lean pay/benefits, teamwork, standard procedures
Innovation (Apple, 3M, pharma): hire for creativity, analysis, teamwork; reward persistence
Porter: advantage = better product at a premium or good product for less

cards.front: What HR approach fits a customer intimacy (customization) strategy?
cards.answer: Hiring and developing people who learn customers' needs and can flex service, often with heavy HR investment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.15 Gaining a Competitive Advantage Through HRM
points: Common in consulting, retail, banking
Starbucks: hires active learners with customer skills and emotional resilience

cards.front: Why do mergers and acquisitions so often fail?
cards.answer: The combining firms' cultures, values, or structures clash, more often than any technical or financial issue.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.15 Gaining a Competitive Advantage Through HRM
points: M&A is a common route to growth and international expansion
Failures: DaimlerChrysler, HP-Compaq, AOL-Time Warner
Check culture fit before the deal

cards.front: Why is every supervising manager responsible for HRM?
cards.answer: HR supplies the tools, but managers use them daily; the system only works if managers apply them well.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.16 Who Is Responsible for HRM?
points: HR is a support function: interview guides, review forms, etc.
Mattel made managers true partners in managing talent
Employees also own pieces: their own development, records, certifications

cards.front: How does a PEO differ from a shared service center?
cards.answer: A PEO is an outside firm that becomes the legal employer; a shared service center is an in-house hub for routine HR.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.16 Who Is Responsible for HRM?
points: PEO: leases workers for ~2-7% of gross wages; handles payroll, benefits, training, discipline
Shared service center: centralizes payroll/benefits transactions (Home Depot HR call centers)
Outsourcing to vendors is a third option, especially for small firms

cards.front: Why did IBM separate core HR roles from administrative ones?
cards.answer: Centralizing routine admin freed HR experts to focus on strategic work like talent, leadership, and upskilling.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.17 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.17 Case Study: HR Transformation at IBM
points: Admin (payroll, expenses, records) moved to global service centers
Also replaced annual reviews with frequent feedback via the employee-designed Checkpoint app
Goal: right talent, right time, right place

cards.front: What is an HRMS, and how should a firm choose one?
cards.answer: A tech platform for employee records, recruiting, and analytics; choose based on real intended use and ease of use.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.19 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.19 Human Resource Management Systems
points: Cloud (Workday, Cornerstone OnDemand) or in-house
Increasingly integrates apps and supports continuous feedback

cards.front: How does Patagonia's HR reinforce its business strategy?
cards.answer: It hires for mission fit and offers cause-driven benefits, building a loyal workforce with very low turnover.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.20 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.20 Real World Response: Patagonia; 1.3 Real World Challenge: Patagonia
points: Paid environmental volunteering, bail for peaceful protest, on-site childcare
Nearly 100% of new mothers return; ~4% turnover; ~9,000 applicants for few openings
Strategy: high-quality, responsibly made gear; 'do well and do good'

cards.front: What does SHRM's code ask of HR professionals?
cards.answer: Act ethically, obey the law, measure HR's impact, and openly advocate for fair treatment of people.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.18 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.18 Ethics in HRM
points: SHRM = largest HR professional association
Professional responsibility: add value, own your decisions, advocate for the profession

cards.front: Exit interviews show new hires at a call center quit because nobody told them the job requires rotating weekend shifts. HR rewrites job postings and adds a realistic job preview. Which HR function is this?
cards.explanation: Defining job requirements and recruiting people who will accept and stay in the role is staffing. Fixing the front end of hiring prevents the turnover.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.6 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.6 Staffing

cards.front: A firm's new strategy needs reps to cross-sell. The reps know how and would earn commission for it, but no one told them it's a priority and their job descriptions still say 'take orders.' Which element is missing?
cards.explanation: They have the ability (can do) and the incentive (will do), but no direction. Planning and job design tell people what they should do.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.4 What Is HRM?

cards.front: A startup's sales reps don't understand the product. The CEO's fix is a huge commission bonus. What's the flaw?
choices: Pay can't supply missing ability; this is a staffing or training gap
Bonuses are a form of indirect compensation
The reps should be moved to a PEO
Nothing; motivation is always the issue
cards.explanation: Incentives affect 'will do,' not 'can do.' If people lack knowledge, you need better hiring or training first.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.4 What Is HRM?; 1.6 Staffing

cards.front: A company pays bonuses only on the number of new accounts opened. Months later an audit finds many accounts were never authorized by customers. What went wrong?
choices: The reward created an incentive to game the metric
cards.explanation: A narrow target rewarded volume regardless of how it was reached. Wells Fargo is the real example. Good 'will do' design anticipates unintended consequences.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.4 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.4 What Is HRM?

cards.front: A hospital trains nurses on a new safety checklist, but annual reviews and raises are based only on patients seen per shift. Nurses skip the checklist. Best diagnosis?
choices: HR functions are misaligned and work against each other
cards.explanation: Training teaches one behavior while performance management and pay reward another. Functions must reinforce the same behaviors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.11 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.11 Employee-Management Relations; 1.7 Training and Development

cards.front: Offer A: $80K, few benefits. Offer B: $74K plus full health coverage, a 6% retirement match, tuition aid, and flexible hours. How should you compare them?
choices: Pick A; salary is what counts
Compare total rewards across both offers
Pick whichever has the bigger bonus
Ignore benefits since they aren't compensation
cards.explanation: Total rewards includes direct pay, benefits (indirect), and nonfinancial rewards. B's benefits may be worth far more than $6K.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.9 Apply · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 1.9 Rewards and Benefits

cards.front: Which of these is indirect financial compensation?
choices: Public recognition at a team meeting
cards.explanation: Indirect financial compensation is benefits like wellness, insurance, and PTO. Bonuses and options are direct; recognition is nonfinancial.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.9 Apply · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 1.9 Rewards and Benefits

cards.front: An employee files a harassment complaint, and HR learns that supervisors were never trained on the anti-harassment policy. Which HR risk is most exposed?
cards.explanation: Harassment, safety, unions, and whistleblowers fall under compliance risk because they involve legal obligations.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?

cards.front: Overtime spending has doubled and payroll errors are causing costly corrections. Which HR risk category is this?
cards.explanation: Pay, overtime, turnover costs, and costly errors are financial risk: the direct money impact of people practices.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?

cards.front: A budget airline competes on the lowest fares. Which HR approach fits its strategy best?
choices: Premium pay to lure star talent
Tight cost control, standard procedures, and teamwork
Hire creative risk-takers and fund experiments
Deep client knowledge and custom service
cards.explanation: Low fares mean an operational excellence strategy: lean costs, consistent procedures, and teamwork on thin margins.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.15 Gaining a Competitive Advantage Through HRM

cards.front: A biotech wants to beat rivals with breakthrough therapies. Which hiring focus fits?
choices: Analytical and creative people who persist through failure
cards.explanation: A product innovation strategy needs an innovative culture and people with analytical and creative ability who keep going through setbacks.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.15 Gaining a Competitive Advantage Through HRM

cards.front: A boutique wealth-management firm wins clients by tailoring advice to each family's situation. Which competitive strategy is this?
cards.explanation: Customization depends on knowing customers deeply and flexing service, so HR invests in hiring and developing people with strong client skills.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.15 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.15 Gaining a Competitive Advantage Through HRM

cards.front: A manager ignores the structured interview guide HR provided and hires on gut feel. The hire flops. Who is most directly responsible?
choices: The manager, because managers carry out HRM day to day
The HR department, since it owns hiring
cards.explanation: HR supplies tools, but they only add value if supervising managers use them. Every manager owns part of HRM.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.16 Who Is Responsible for HRM?

cards.front: A 40-person landscaping company has no HR staff. It wants payroll, benefits, and workers' comp handled, plus the flexibility to shrink its workforce in winter. Best option?
cards.explanation: A PEO becomes the legal employer, handles payroll, benefits, and admin, and lets the client simply not renew leased workers in a downturn.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.16 Who Is Responsible for HRM?

cards.front: A 30,000-employee retailer has every store handling its own payroll and benefits questions, with inconsistent results. They want to keep the work in-house. Best fix?
cards.explanation: Shared service centers centralize routine HR transactions in-house, cutting redundancy and cost while improving consistency.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.16 Who Is Responsible for HRM?

cards.front: A VP pressures an HR manager to quietly bury an employee's safety complaint. What do SHRM's ethical standards point toward?
choices: Comply, since the VP outranks HR
Refuse and raise it through proper channels, protecting legal compliance and fair treatment
Leak it to the media right away
Drop it, since safety isn't an HR issue
cards.explanation: SHRM's code calls for obeying the law, high ethical standards, and openly advocating for proper treatment of people through appropriate forums.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.18 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.18 Ethics in HRM

cards.front: A U.S. firm opens an office in a high power-distance country and launches a 'challenge your boss' empowerment program. Few employees take part. Likely reason?
choices: The program clashes with local norms about hierarchy
cards.explanation: In high power-distance cultures, people expect clear hierarchy, so empowerment programs can feel inappropriate. Fit HR practices to the local culture.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.14 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.14 Global Issues

cards.front: A company is choosing an HRMS. Which factor should matter most?
choices: How the firm will actually use it and how easy it is for managers and employees
cards.explanation: Pick an HRMS for its real intended use and ease of use. Unused features add cost without adding value.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.19 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.19 Human Resource Management Systems

cards.front: A CEO worries that fast growth has weakened the company's ethics and culture. Which category of HR risk is this?
cards.explanation: Talent strategy, culture, ethics awareness, and change all fall under strategic risk.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12 Practice · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?

cards.front: For HR functions to support rather than undermine each other, they need to be consistent in...
choices: How long they've been in place
cards.explanation: Alignment means every function, from hiring and training to pay and reviews, pushes toward the same behaviors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.11 Practice · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.11 Employee-Management Relations

cards.front: Small businesses most often report which two areas as their biggest management problems?
cards.explanation: Recruitment and training are top problems, especially for small firms with no HR budget. That's why HR is an investment, not just a cost.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.7 Practice · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.7 Training and Development; 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?

cards.front: A company is restructuring and downsizing. Which group is usually expected to lead the organizational change?
cards.explanation: HR professionals lead organizational change like expansion, restructuring, and downsizing, using communication, influence, and leadership skills.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.16 Practice · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.16 Who Is Responsible for HRM?

cards.front: When you boil it down, what is HRM ultimately trying to do for a company?
choices: Be the main contact for shareholders
Reduce people-related risk and keep strong performers
cards.explanation: HRM manages people risk (legal, financial, strategic) and builds a talent system that keeps great employees. The other options belong to other functions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q1 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.4 What Is HRM?

cards.front: A CFO asks how HR actually creates value. What's the best answer?
choices: Hiring only people with advanced degrees
Helping the company carry out its business strategy
Keeping pay as low as possible
cards.explanation: HRM creates value by helping execute business strategy, getting the right people with the right skills and motivation in place.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q2 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.13 The Role of HRM in Executing Business Strategy; 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?

cards.front: Which sequence best captures HRM's core purpose across the employee life cycle?
cards.explanation: HRM attracts, hires, develops, rewards, and retains talent. Each verb maps to an HR function.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q3 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.4 What Is HRM?

cards.front: A plant switches to a new assembly process, and workers need new skills to run it. Which HR function steps in?
cards.explanation: Building current employees' skills for new methods is training and development. Staffing would bring in new people instead.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q4 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.7 Training and Development

cards.front: Staffing isn't just filling seats. It exists to help the company carry out its ___ strategy.
cards.explanation: Staffing plans, acquires, deploys, and retains talent so the firm can execute its business strategy.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q5 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.6 Staffing

cards.front: Layoffs, resignations, and firings for poor performance fall under which HR function?
cards.explanation: Staffing moves talent into, through, AND out of the organization, so separations are part of it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q6 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.6 Staffing

cards.front: A company grooms several high-potential managers years in advance so it's ready if the COO leaves. What is this called?
cards.explanation: Succession planning prepares people to fill key positions and reduces disruption during transitions (think Google and Pichai).
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q7 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.7 Training and Development

cards.front: Which HR function makes sure what individual employees aim for lines up with what the organization is trying to achieve?
cards.explanation: Performance management aligns employee goals and behavior with organizational goals, then appraises and improves performance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.8 Performance Management

cards.front: If staffing brings in the wrong people, which two other functions feel the impact most directly?
cards.explanation: Staffing supplies the raw talent. Development has to fill the gaps, and performance management depends on that talent being there.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q9 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.8 Performance Management; 1.6 Staffing

cards.front: A manager wants to reinforce ethical conduct day to day. According to the chapter, which kind of feedback serves that purpose?
cards.explanation: Performance feedback, part of performance management, tells people how they're doing, communicates expectations, and helps maintain ethical behavior.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q10 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.8 Performance Management

cards.front: A job offer lists base salary, a signing bonus, sales commission, and stock options. Together these are...
cards.explanation: Salary, wages, commissions, bonuses, and stock options are direct financial compensation, paid directly for work.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q11 · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 1.9 Rewards and Benefits

cards.front: Employer-paid health insurance, paid vacation, and a retirement plan are examples of...
cards.explanation: Benefits are indirect financial compensation: they have money value but aren't paid as cash for performance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q12 · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 1.9 Rewards and Benefits

cards.front: An analyst says the best part of her job is the sense of accomplishment and feeling appreciated by her team. Which reward category is that?
cards.explanation: Intrinsic rewards from the work or environment, like feeling successful or valued, are nonfinancial compensation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q13 · Motivational Concepts
cards.note: Read more: 1.9 Rewards and Benefits

cards.front: One major way effective HRM boosts organizational performance is by building...
cards.explanation: HRM adds value by improving efficiency (efficient systems and processes) and by contributing to revenue growth.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q14 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?

cards.front: Three of these are outcomes of an effective HRM system. Which one is NOT?
choices: Tying rewards fairly to responsibility and performance
Reporting ethics violations to the Bureau of Labor Statistics
cards.explanation: The BLS is a statistics agency; reporting ethics breaches to it isn't an HRM outcome. The others are listed benefits of effective HRM.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q15 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?

cards.front: The strategy that defines where and how a company competes in its market is its ___ strategy.
cards.explanation: Business strategy is how a firm competes and positions itself. HR strategy must then fit it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q16 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.13 The Role of HRM in Executing Business Strategy

cards.front: A founder believes employees are long-term partners worth investing in, not interchangeable parts. This set of beliefs about how people should be treated is the company's...
cards.explanation: A talent philosophy is the firm's beliefs about how employees should be treated. It guides the integrated HRM system. ('Employee philosophy' is the tempting wrong pick.)
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q17 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.13 The Role of HRM in Executing Business Strategy

cards.front: Which approach do firms commonly use to expand quickly into new countries?
cards.explanation: Mergers and acquisitions are a common route to growth and international expansion, and a way to acquire talent.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q18 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.15 Gaining a Competitive Advantage Through HRM

cards.front: Two companies merge. The deal looks great on paper but falls apart within two years. What's the most common culprit?
cards.explanation: M&A deals most often fail because cultures, values, or structures clash (DaimlerChrysler, AOL-Time Warner).
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q19 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.15 Gaining a Competitive Advantage Through HRM

cards.front: Which document is the go-to reference that helps employees understand company HR policies?
cards.explanation: Employee handbooks, often online, document HR policies and serve as a reference for employees.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1 Quiz Q20 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.16 Who Is Responsible for HRM?

cards.front: What are the six primary HRM functions?
cards.answer: Staffing, training & development, performance management, rewards & benefits, health & safety, employee relations.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.5 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.5 What Does HRM Do?; 1.6 Staffing
points: Staffing: plan, acquire, deploy, retain, and separate talent
Training and development: build skills, careers, and successors
Performance management: align goals, appraise, give feedback
Rewards and benefits: direct pay, benefits, nonfinancial rewards
Health and safety: protect physical and mental well-being
Employee-management relations: rights, voice, unions

cards.front: Why is HRM a strategic investment for both small and large firms?
cards.answer: People are a top cost, so better hiring, training, and retention raise productivity and profit at any size.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?; 1.4 What Is HRM?
points: Model answer: HR cuts costly turnover, lawsuits, and errors, and builds skills that improve service and quality
Large firms: efficiency and revenue growth; Moody's even weighs HR in bond ratings
Small firms: poor HR practices are a leading cause of failure, and recruiting and training are their top problems
Costco shows that spending more on people can pay for itself

cards.front: A software company recruits and trains engineers to write secure, well-tested code, but sprint bonuses are paid only for the number of features shipped. What is the most likely result?
choices: The bonus will quietly undo the hiring and training investment, as engineers trade quality for volume
The functions will balance out because training outweighs pay
The strategy will be carried out faster and better
Engineers will ignore the bonus because they were trained on quality
cards.explanation: When rewards conflict with what staffing and training aim for, people follow the rewards. Misaligned functions undermine each other and the strategy.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.11 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.11 Employee-Management Relations; 1.7 Training and Development

cards.front: A hotel chain holds monthly town halls, runs an anonymous employee survey, and sets up a joint labor-management committee to resolve complaints early. Which HR function is this?
cards.explanation: Employee voice programs, surveys, and union or labor relations belong to employee-management relations. Good relations improve communication and problem solving.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.11 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.11 Employee-Management Relations

cards.front: A distribution center installs lift-assist equipment, trains workers on safe lifting, and tracks injuries by shift. Which HR function is this, and what's the business payoff?
choices: Rewards and benefits; higher pay satisfaction
Health and safety; fewer lost workdays and lower workers' comp costs
cards.explanation: This is health and safety. Beyond being ethical, it raises productivity and lowers insurance, workers' comp, and lost-time costs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.10 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.10 Health and Safety

cards.front: The owner of a 25-person firm calls HR 'overhead' while turnover runs 60% a year and new hires take months to get up to speed. Which argument best shows why HRM matters to performance?
choices: HR is required by law at every firm
HR mainly helps by keeping wages low
Big companies need HR, but small ones don't
Better hiring and training would cut replacement costs and lift productivity
cards.explanation: HRM adds value through efficiency and revenue growth at any size. Poor people practices are a leading cause of small-firm failure, so HR is an investment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.12 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.12 How Does HRM Influence Organizational Performance?

cards.front: A retailer switches its strategy from lowest price to premium, personalized service, but keeps hiring for speed and paying the lowest wages in town. What is the most likely strategic impact?
choices: The new strategy stalls because HR practices no longer fit it
Costs fall, so the premium strategy succeeds
Nothing changes, since strategy is set by executives, not HR
cards.explanation: HR must fit the business strategy. A customer-intimacy strategy needs people with service skills and the pay and training to keep them; low-cost HR undermines it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 1.13 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 1.13 The Role of HRM in Executing Business Strategy
